stem: Which statement correctly describes the core Terraform workflow?

choices.text: Write configuration as code, plan to preview the proposed changes, then apply to provision the infrastructure.
Draft the resources in the console, export them to a state file, then run a test suite to approve the release.
Initialize the backend, validate against the provider APIs, then deploy the changes straight to the target environment.
Plan the desired state, write the plan file by hand, then apply it after a manual review by the provider.

stem: A teammate cloned a repository that already has an initialized working directory. Before running `terraform plan`, which TWO things should you expect the plan to do by default? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Create the missing resources so the infrastructure matches the configuration.
Read the current state of existing remote objects to check that the state is up to date.
Compare the current configuration with the prior state and note the differences.
Format the configuration files so they follow the canonical style.
Rewrite the dependency lock file with the newest provider versions available.

stem: An apply that creates a network, a subnet and a database fails on the database with a quota error. The network and subnet were created successfully. What is the state of things and what should you do?

choices.text: Terraform locked the workspace permanently, so you must destroy everything before attempting another apply.
Terraform discarded the state update, so you must import the network and subnet before the next apply.
Terraform rolled back the network and subnet, so you can run the same apply again from a clean start.
Terraform recorded the network and subnet in state and left them in place, so fix the cause and apply again.

stem: A developer runs `terraform plan` with no options and later wants to run exactly what was shown. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The plan locked the state until the next apply, so another engineer cannot plan in the meantime.
The plan was written to the `.terraform` directory, so `terraform apply -auto-approve` is required to use it.
The plan was saved automatically, so `terraform apply` will reuse it without recalculating anything.
The plan was speculative, and `terraform apply` generates a new plan that you approve before it executes.

stem: A new engineer asks what `terraform init` does in a freshly cloned repository. Which TWO activities are part of initialization? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Compares configuration against real infrastructure and prints a list of proposed changes.
Creates the infrastructure described by the configuration and writes the first state snapshot.
Initializes the configured backend so that state can be read and stored.
Checks every resource argument against the remote provider API for valid values.
Installs the provider plugins the configuration needs and records the selections in the dependency lock file.

stem: The lock file pins a provider to 5.40.0, and the configuration constraint is `~> 5.0`. You want the newest 5.x release. Which command does that?

choices.text: `terraform init -upgrade`
`terraform plan -refresh-only`
`terraform apply -replace=provider`
`terraform init -reconfigure`

stem: A configuration has used the default local backend. A `backend "s3"` block is added, and the existing state must move to the bucket. Which command accomplishes this?

choices.text: `terraform init -reconfigure`
`terraform init -migrate-state`
`terraform init -backend=false`
`terraform apply -refresh-only`

stem: After an engineer edited the bucket name in a `backend "s3"` block, `terraform plan` reports that the backend configuration has changed. The new bucket is intentionally empty and the old state must not be copied. Which action is correct?

choices.text: Run `terraform init -migrate-state` and answer yes to every prompt so the old state is copied across.
Run `terraform init -reconfigure` to use the new settings and not migrate existing state.
Delete the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file and run `terraform plan` again without re-initializing.
Run `terraform init -upgrade` to refresh the plugins and re-read the backend settings.

stem: A CI job should check a module before any credentials exist. Backend access must not be attempted, but providers must be installed. Which command prepares the directory?

choices.text: `terraform init -input=false`
`terraform init -get=false`
`terraform init -lock=false`
`terraform init -backend=false`

stem: A configuration uses a registry module with `version = "~> 3.0"`. Version 3.1 is installed. Version 3.2 is released, and an engineer re-runs `terraform init`. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Init keeps the installed module and installs only newly added modules, unless `-upgrade` is used.
Init always replaces every installed module with the newest release that the version constraint allows.
Init fails with an error, because modules can be installed only once in a working directory.
Init updates the module only when `terraform get -update` has been run beforehand to unlock it.

stem: A team wants a fast pre-commit check that needs no cloud credentials. Which statement about `terraform validate` is accurate?

choices.text: It requires the input variables to have values, otherwise it exits with an error.
It compares the configuration with the state and reports the create, update and destroy actions that a plan would propose.
It checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent, without contacting remote services.
It queries provider APIs to confirm that the named resources and credentials are usable.

stem: In a new clone, `terraform validate` stops with errors saying that required providers and modules are not installed. The code itself has not been changed. What is the next step?

choices.text: Run `terraform init` (or `terraform init -backend=false`), then run `terraform validate` again.
Run `terraform fmt -recursive` so the modules are normalized, downloaded and installed in place.
Run `terraform plan -refresh-only` so that the missing plugins are downloaded and cached.
Run `terraform apply -auto-approve` so that Terraform installs the missing plugins and modules on the way.

stem: Which TWO problems can `terraform validate` detect? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Credentials that lack the permission needed to create the configured resource type.
An expression that refers to `var.region` when no such variable is declared.
An AMI ID that does not exist in the target region of the provider.
A storage bucket name that is already taken by another account.
A `resource` block that uses an argument name the provider schema does not define.

stem: A pipeline must apply exactly the changes that reviewers approved in a pull request. Which approach does this?

choices.text: Run `terraform validate -out=tfplan`, then `terraform apply -target=tfplan`.
Run `terraform plan` in review, then `terraform apply -auto-approve` later with the same options.
Run `terraform plan -refresh-only` in review, then `terraform apply` in the apply stage.
Run `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, then run `terraform apply tfplan` in the apply stage.

stem: Which statement about `-target` on `terraform plan` is accurate?

choices.text: It works only together with `-destroy`, as planning an update cannot be restricted.
It is the recommended routine way to split a large configuration into parts.
It focuses the plan on the matching instances and their dependencies, and is for exceptional cases.
It limits the plan to the named resource only, and ignores any other resource that it depends on directly.

stem: During an incident, an engineer changed a tag on a load balancer in the console. The change is intended to stay. Which command shows how Terraform would update only its records to match, without proposing changes to the load balancer?

choices.text: `terraform plan -refresh=false`
`terraform plan -refresh-only`
`terraform plan -destroy`
`terraform plan -target=aws_lb.main`

stem: A teammate wants to combine plan options in one run and asks which rules apply. Which statement about planning modes is accurate?

choices.text: Normal mode is the default; destroy and refresh-only are alternative modes and cannot be used together.
Refresh-only is the default mode because every plan begins by synchronizing state first.
`-replace` can be combined with `-destroy` to rebuild one resource and remove the rest.
The modes can be combined, so `-destroy -refresh-only` destroys and refreshes together.

stem: A CI job should fail a scheduled run whenever Terraform would make changes, but should not fail for an empty plan. Which option supports this?

choices.text: `terraform plan -input=false`, treating any non-zero exit code as changes present
`terraform validate -json`, treating a non-empty result as changes present
`terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`, treating exit code 2 as changes present
`terraform plan -lock=false`, treating a shorter run time as no changes

stem: A plan includes this entry for `aws_instance.web`: `-/+ resource "aws_instance" "web" (forces replacement)`. What will Terraform do if applied?

choices.text: Add a second instance and keep the existing one.
Update the instance in place, leaving its ID unchanged.
Remove the instance from state only, leaving the real instance running.
Destroy the existing instance and create a new one in its place.

stem: Plans for a very large configuration take a long time because of many API reads, and an engineer proposes `terraform plan -refresh=false`. Which statement describes the trade-off?

choices.text: Plans become safer, because skipping the refresh prevents any state change by the run.
Plans become faster, but external changes to remote objects may go unnoticed, so the plan may be incorrect.
Plans become slower, because Terraform compares each resource twice against the state file.
Plans become faster, and Terraform still detects external changes by using the cached schema.

stem: An engineer runs `terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan` on a saved plan file. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Terraform skips only non-destructive operations from the file, as `-auto-approve` excludes deletions.
Terraform prompts anyway, because saved plans always require interactive confirmation.
Terraform re-plans first, because `-auto-approve` discards the saved file.
Terraform ignores `-auto-approve`, because passing a saved plan file is already treated as approval.

stem: A script runs `terraform apply -target=aws_s3_bucket.logs tfplan` and Terraform rejects the command. What explains this?

choices.text: Planning options cannot be added when applying a saved plan, because the file already holds the final decisions.
`-target` is allowed only with `terraform destroy` and is never accepted on any apply.
Saved plans cannot be used until `terraform validate` has produced a marker file in the working directory.
The `tfplan` file has expired after a time limit, so it must be regenerated first.

stem: A pipeline step runs `terraform apply -input=false` and fails because Terraform cannot ask for confirmation. Which TWO changes let the job run unattended? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add `-lock=false` so that Terraform skips the approval prompt.
Add `-refresh=false` so there is no plan to approve.
Add `-auto-approve` to apply, after a separate reviewed plan.
Run `terraform validate` before apply so Terraform marks the configuration as approved.
Run `terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false` first, then `terraform apply tfplan`.

stem: Immediately after a successful apply, an engineer runs `terraform apply` again with no code changes. It prints "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration." What does this mean?

choices.text: Terraform skipped refresh, so it could not compare anything.
Terraform locked the configuration, so more applies are blocked until a change is committed.
The plan found no differences between the configuration, state and real objects, so nothing is changed.
The previous apply failed silently, so Terraform did not write state.

stem: Before a change window, a reviewer is handed a saved plan file `tfplan` and must see what it will do without applying it. Which command works?

choices.text: `terraform fmt tfplan`
`terraform init tfplan`
`terraform validate tfplan`
`terraform show tfplan`

stem: A new team member wants to tear down a test stack and asks how `terraform destroy` works. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It is a convenience alias for `terraform apply -destroy`, and does not accept a plan file argument.
It removes only the state file and leaves the remote objects running.
It requires a saved plan, which is created by `terraform plan -out` first.
It deletes every resource in the cloud account, including resources not managed by the configuration.

stem: A team wants a reviewed teardown of a test environment, where the destroy plan is saved, inspected, and applied later. Which sequence works?

choices.text: `terraform destroy -out=destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform destroy destroy.tfplan`
`terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform apply destroy.tfplan`
`terraform plan -refresh-only -out=destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform apply destroy.tfplan`
`terraform apply -out=destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform destroy -auto-approve`

stem: An engineer ran `terraform destroy` on a stack; a VM created by hand in the same subnet is still running afterward. Why?

choices.text: The destroy ran in refresh-only mode, which never removes any resources from the environment.
Terraform destroys only objects tracked in its state, and the VM created by hand is not one of them.
`destroy` skips resources that have network dependencies.
Terraform destroys resources only in the order listed, and the VM was not reached yet.

stem: A CI step must fail when any `.tf` file in the repository, including modules in subfolders, is not canonically formatted, and must not change any files. Which TWO options belong in the command? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `-recursive`, which also processes files in subdirectories.
`-lock=false`, which prevents concurrent edits to the files.
`-backend=false`, which stops the formatter reading the state.
`-upgrade`, which brings subdirectory modules up to date.
`-check`, which exits non-zero and lists unformatted files without rewriting them.

stem: An engineer runs `terraform fmt` in a directory that has a `modules/` subfolder, with no options. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It changes resource names so that they match the style guide.
It rewrites every file in all subfolders, because recursion is the default behavior of the formatter.
It rewrites files in the current directory in place and lists them, but does not touch files in the subfolder.
It only reports problems and leaves all files unchanged.

stem: A reviewer wants to see what `terraform fmt` would change in `main.tf` without modifying the file. Which command does that?

choices.text: `terraform fmt -upgrade main.tf` to print the style changes
`terraform validate -diff main.tf` to print the style differences
`terraform plan -fmt main.tf` to print the style changes
`terraform fmt -diff -write=false main.tf`

stem: A team replaces its console click-through runbook with files that describe each network, server and DNS record. Which statement best defines what they have adopted?

choices.text: Disaster recovery: a standby copy of every resource is kept in a second region so that it can take over
Continuous monitoring: a tool samples running resources and raises alerts when utilization crosses a threshold
Configuration drift: real infrastructure slowly stops matching the original runbook and is hard to rebuild
Infrastructure as code: infrastructure described in readable files that are versioned, reviewed and applied by a tool

stem: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a declarative and an imperative approach to provisioning infrastructure?

choices.text: Declarative tools take the desired end state and derive the steps, while imperative tools take the ordered steps
A declarative tool supports only one cloud vendor, while an imperative tool works with any vendor through scripts
A declarative tool must be run from a console, while an imperative tool can only be run from a command line
Declarative tools rerun every instruction on each execution, while imperative tools skip steps already done

stem: An engineer reads this configuration and asks what Terraform does when it is applied twice in a row with no edits. resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" { bucket = "acme-audit-logs" } What happens on the second apply?

choices.text: Terraform creates a second bucket with the same name and fails with a duplicate error
Terraform asks for the bucket name again because it does not remember the previous run
Terraform finds the bucket already matches the configuration and proposes no changes
Terraform deletes the bucket and creates it again so the result is predictable

stem: Which statement about the role of Terraform providers in the IaC workflow is accurate?

choices.text: Providers are state files that record the remote identifier of every managed resource
Providers are plugins that translate resource definitions into API calls to a platform or service
Providers are cloud accounts that must be created before Terraform can read any configuration file
Providers are reusable folders of configuration that package several resources behind input variables

stem: A company wants to manage a Datadog monitor, a GitHub repository and a DNS record with the same tool it uses for virtual machines. Which statement explains why Terraform can do this?

choices.text: Terraform can only manage services that run on a hypervisor operated by the cloud vendor
Terraform ships built-in resource types for every SaaS product inside the CLI binary itself
Terraform scans the environment and automatically adopts every service it discovers
Terraform manages anything that has an accessible API and a provider, not only compute, storage and networking

stem: A team lead says, "Terraform is our configuration manager, so we will use it to install packages and edit config files inside running servers." Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Terraform and configuration managers are the same category, so the choice between them is purely a matter of syntax preference
Terraform mainly provisions infrastructure, while in-guest setup usually belongs to Ansible, Chef or Puppet
Terraform can manage in-guest software only when the servers run on-premises, not in a public cloud
Terraform replaces in-guest tools because providers include package and service resources for the operating system

stem: Which statements correctly describe the "write, plan, apply" workflow that Terraform brings to IaC? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Apply performs the proposed operations in dependency order once the plan is approved
Write is the stage where Terraform contacts every provider and creates the declared resources
Plan automatically changes resources whose arguments differ so that apply has less work to do
Apply must be preceded by a manual export of the remote state to a local file
Plan produces an execution plan describing what will be created, updated or destroyed, based on the configuration and existing infrastructure

stem: Terraform's overview says it "takes an immutable approach to infrastructure". Which practice is consistent with that approach?

choices.text: Store the patch commands in the configuration so Terraform replays them on the existing server at each apply
Sign in to each running server and patch it in place, then leave the configuration files as they were
Change the definition and apply it so Terraform updates or replaces the resource, instead of hand-patching the running server
Keep one long-lived server per environment and never allow Terraform to replace any resource

stem: Which statement about the language used to write Terraform configuration is accurate?

choices.text: Configuration must be written as Go programs that are compiled before they can be planned
Configuration is written as a sequence of shell commands that Terraform runs line by line from top to bottom
Configuration is stored only as binary plan files that cannot be read by humans
Configuration is written in HCL, a declarative language, with a JSON-compatible syntax also available

stem: A team writes this configuration. Which statement describes how Terraform decides the creation order? resource "aws_subnet" "app" { vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24" } resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" }

choices.text: The subnet is created first because it appears first in the file
Terraform asks the operator which resource to create first
The VPC id reference creates a dependency, so the VPC is created first despite appearing later
Both resources are created in an arbitrary order, and the subnet is retried automatically until the VPC exists

stem: Which TWO statements correctly contrast managing infrastructure through a cloud console with managing it through IaC? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A console keeps a reviewable history of intended changes, while an IaC file has no history
Console changes are hard to reproduce exactly, while an IaC definition can be applied again to build the same infrastructure
IaC works only when the infrastructure is created for the first time and cannot be used for later changes
Console work scales to hundreds of identical environments more easily than an IaC definition does
IaC definitions can be reviewed before they take effect, while a console click takes effect immediately

stem: A company must create identical development, test and production networks and wants to avoid subtle differences between them. Which IaC benefit addresses this?

choices.text: Repeatability: one definition with different inputs yields the same structure in every environment
Encryption at rest: data stored in all three environments is encrypted by default with provider-managed keys
Latency routing: users are directed to the environment closest to them
Elasticity: the platform automatically adds capacity to each network as load grows

stem: After an outage, a manager asks "who changed the firewall rule and why?" The team keeps its Terraform files in Git. How does that help?

choices.text: Git automatically blocks any firewall change that has not been approved by the cloud provider
The cloud provider copies each Git commit into its own audit service, so no commit history is needed
Each rule change is a commit with an author, timestamp, message and usually a reviewed pull request
Terraform rewrites the configuration to remove old rules, so the question no longer applies

stem: Over the weekend someone added an inbound port rule in the console to a security group whose rules are defined in the Terraform configuration. On Monday the team runs a plan with no configuration edits. What should they expect?

choices.text: The plan notices the port no longer matches the configuration and proposes to change it back
The plan deletes the whole server because any manual edit marks the resource as unmanaged
The plan updates the configuration file to include the new port so that the two agree
The plan reports no changes because Terraform never contacts the provider during planning

stem: A software vendor wants prospects to try its product on their own cloud account and to choose parameters such as cluster size. Which statement describes why defining the demo as Terraform configuration helps?

choices.text: The vendor must create every prospect environment in its own account, because configuration cannot target another account
Prospects apply the same definition, adjust input values, and get a consistent environment without manual setup steps
Prospects follow a written click-by-click guide, which gives the same result as an applied definition
Prospects receive a prebuilt virtual machine image, because configuration files cannot contain adjustable values

stem: Which TWO practices make an IaC workflow safer for a team that shares infrastructure? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Apply first and read the results afterwards, because a plan cannot predict anything useful
Let each engineer apply changes from a laptop with no review so that fixes are never delayed
Edit resources in the console during incidents and never record the change in code
Run a plan and read it for unexpected destroys or replacements before approving an apply
Keep configuration in version control and require review of changes before they are applied

stem: A central operations team receives many repetitive requests for the same kind of infrastructure. Which Terraform capability best supports a self-service model that still follows company standards?

choices.text: Reusable modules that package the approved build of a service, called by teams with their own inputs
A provider plugin written for each product team so that the CLI changes its syntax
A single shared configuration file that all teams edit directly in the same place
A ticket queue in which the operations team hand-writes a new configuration for each individual request

stem: Which statement about the Terraform state file and the benefit it gives an IaC workflow is accurate?

choices.text: State replaces the need to write any configuration, because Terraform infers the desired resources from it alone
State is a full backup of the cloud account's data that is used to restore deleted resources
State is the list of providers a team is allowed to download from the registry
State records the real objects Terraform manages, so it can compute changes to match the configuration

stem: A QA team needs a full copy of the production stack for three days of testing. Which statement describes the IaC benefit?

choices.text: Build it by hand once and keep it running permanently so that results stay comparable
Create it from the existing definition, use it, then destroy it with the same tooling to avoid idle cost
The copy is created by exporting production data files and importing them into a new account
Terraform can only create a copy when the original stack is shut down first

stem: A change lowers the instance count from 3 to 2 and also changes an AMI id. A reviewer wants to be sure the apply will not destroy more than expected. What should the reviewer rely on?

choices.text: The cloud billing page, which shows what will be deleted by the next apply
The previous apply output, because plans are always identical to earlier runs
The execution plan, which lists each resource to be created, updated, replaced or destroyed before apply
The pull request title, because Terraform validates titles against the generated plan before it is applied

stem: Which statement best describes how Terraform handles infrastructure across several cloud platforms?

choices.text: A single resource type automatically works on every cloud, so the same block can be switched between vendors without edits
Terraform needs a separate installation and a different command set for each cloud vendor
One configuration and workflow can use several providers, each implementing its own platform's API
Terraform copies running workloads between clouds when one vendor has an outage

stem: A configuration declares these providers and resources. What does Terraform do with it? provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" } provider "google" { project = "acme-prod" } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { bucket = "acme-assets" } resource "google_storage_bucket" "backup" { name     = "acme-backup" location = "US" }

choices.text: It creates both buckets in AWS because the first provider block sets the default for everything
It requires two separate runs, one for each cloud, with no way to combine them
It rejects the configuration because one working directory can use only a single provider
It creates the bucket in each platform through the matching provider in a single plan and apply

stem: A team moves a workload from AWS to Azure by changing only the provider block in a configuration that contains aws_instance resources. The plan fails. What explains this?

choices.text: Resource types belong to one provider, so aws_instance blocks must be rewritten as Azure resource types
The state file always blocks provider changes until it is deleted by hand
The provider block must be spelled with capital letters to be accepted
Terraform cannot connect to Azure at all, because multi-cloud workflows are not supported by the tool

stem: A company runs virtual machines on a VMware vSphere cluster in its data center and also uses a public cloud for storage. Which statement about managing both with Terraform is accurate?

choices.text: Terraform needs a separate on-premises CLI edition that cannot read the same configuration language
Terraform manages both in one workflow, with a provider for the on-premises platform and one for the cloud
Terraform manages only public cloud services and cannot reach on-premises systems
Terraform requires the on-premises cluster to be moved to the public cloud first

stem: A web tier in a public cloud needs a DNS record whose value is the load balancer address, and the DNS zone is hosted at a different vendor. How does Terraform handle this cross-platform dependency?

choices.text: The DNS resource references the load balancer's address, so Terraform creates the load balancer first
The DNS record is created first with a placeholder, and Terraform later swaps the value in a background job
Terraform cannot express dependencies between resources that belong to different providers
An operator must create the load balancer, copy its address manually, then run Terraform for the DNS record

stem: Which TWO statements about the Terraform Registry and providers are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Providers are bundled inside the Terraform CLI download and cannot be updated separately
Providers are only available for the three largest public clouds
The public Terraform Registry lists thousands of providers for clouds, SaaS products and on-premises platforms
Only providers written by HashiCorp can be used with Terraform
You can write your own provider for an internal system that has an API

stem: A security team asks why Terraform is described as "service-agnostic" rather than "cloud-agnostic". Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It replaces each service's own API with a single universal API owned by HashiCorp
It manages any API-backed service through a provider, including DNS, monitoring and source hosting
It guarantees that any configuration runs unchanged on every service in its provider catalog, with no rewriting
It is limited to the services of one vendor so that behavior stays consistent

stem: Which statement describes a reason an organization might choose a multi-cloud strategy with Terraform, and the challenge Terraform addresses?

choices.text: Multi-cloud makes all state files unnecessary because each cloud tracks its own resources
Multi-cloud lowers prices because Terraform picks the cheapest vendor for each resource
Multi-cloud removes the need for any provider credentials because Terraform logs in as the organization
Multiple clouds can improve fault tolerance, and Terraform eases the added complexity with one workflow

stem: A platform team manages a Kubernetes cluster and the applications on it. Which statements correctly describe how Terraform fits? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Terraform replaces the Kubernetes API, so kubectl and existing manifests stop working entirely
Terraform manages only the cluster itself, and each deployment inside it must use another tool
Terraform can manage Kubernetes only when the cluster runs on-premises rather than in a cloud
A cloud provider can create the cluster, and the Kubernetes or Helm providers can manage resources in it
One configuration can hold the cloud and Kubernetes providers, so cluster-to-workload dependencies are handled

stem: A team keeps configuration in Git and wants Terraform runs to execute in a consistent environment with shared state, secure secret handling and role-based access controls. Which HashiCorp offering does the Terraform documentation point to?

choices.text: The Terraform Registry, which executes plans for every user who downloads a module
Sentinel, which replaces the plan and apply stages with a single approval step
HCP Terraform, which runs Terraform consistently and manages shared state, secrets and access across teams
A provider plugin, which stores the team's secrets and enforces role-based access in the CLI

stem: An organization wants guardrails so that product teams can create infrastructure themselves but cannot provision disallowed resource types. Which statement matches what HashiCorp documents for this goal?

choices.text: Policy as code, such as Sentinel in HCP Terraform, enforces compliance rules automatically before changes
Terraform CLI alone blocks all non-approved resources without any extra configuration
Cloud vendors automatically disable their Terraform provider for any team that lacks a manager's approval
Teams must open a ticket for each request because policy cannot be automated
